opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a good question, and I'll answer it from the angle of what we're trying to do with physical AI and world foundation models like Cosmos.

When people look at CUDA today, they see a dominant platform and assume it was obvious from the start. It wasn't. When NVIDIA started investing in CUDA, around 2006, there wasn't a clear market for general-purpose GPU computing. A lot of people internally and externally questioned why we'd spend so much engineering effort making GPUs programmable for scientists and researchers when the business was gaming. Jensen's view was that if you build the right platform and make it accessible, the developers will come and find applications you can't predict. Then deep learning happened, AlexNet was trained on GPUs, and suddenly CUDA was the foundation of a whole new industry. But that took years of patience before the payoff.

So when I think about replicating that success, there are a few lessons.

First, you have to invest before the market is obvious. For physical AI, for robotics, autonomous vehicles, and embodied agents, we're roughly where deep learning was before AlexNet. The technology is promising, but the "ChatGPT moment" for robotics hasn't fully arrived. If you wait until it's obvious, you're too late.

Second, a platform has to solve a real bottleneck for developers. For CUDA, the bottleneck was compute. In physical AI, one major bottleneck is data. You can't scrape the internet for robot interaction data the way you can for text. Collecting real-world data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous. A world model that understands physics and can generate realistic, controllable simulations of the world lets developers produce the data they need and test their policies safely. That's the kind of fundamental problem a platform needs to address.

Third, openness and ecosystem matter enormously. CUDA succeeded because there were libraries, documentation, education programs, and a huge community building on top of it. That's why we've released Cosmos models with open weights and a permissive license, along with tokenizers, data curation pipelines, and post-training tools. We want robotics companies, AV companies, and researchers to fine-tune these models for their own domains. A platform is only as strong as what people build on it.

And finally, you need to stay committed through the full stack. CUDA wasn't a single release. It's been refined for almost twenty years, with cuDNN, cuBLAS, and many other layers co-designed with the hardware. For physical AI, we think about the whole loop: training in the data center, simulation with Omniverse and world models, and deployment on edge computers in the robot or car. Each piece makes the others more valuable.

So I wouldn't say we're trying to copy CUDA exactly. The domain is different. But the philosophy is the same: identify the foundational problem, build general tools that empower many developers, open them up, and be patient. If we do that well, I believe physical AI could become as transformative as accelerated computing has been.

r001.rationale: It says CUDA was underway before a clear market existed, then deep learning and AlexNet made CUDA the foundation of a new industry.

r002.rationale: It says the domain is different and they are not copying CUDA exactly, but it does not judge that following CUDA’s original development path is unlikely to reproduce its success.

r003.rationale: It adapts the platform effort to physical AI’s current bottleneck—data—rather than CUDA’s compute bottleneck, and recommends building tools around that need.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we think about a lot, because CUDA is the thing everyone points to when they ask why NVIDIA is where it is. But I'd push back a little on the word "replicating." CUDA wasn't a plan that was executed; it was a bet that got nurtured for fifteen years before it paid off.

If you go back to 2006, 2007, there was no clear reason to put a general-purpose programming model on a graphics chip. Jensen did it anyway. For years CUDA was basically a cost center. Wall Street hated it. What made it work was not the technology alone, it was patience: shipping it on every GPU, including consumer cards, so a graduate student with a gaming machine could program it. Then teaching it in universities, writing the libraries, cuBLAS, cuDNN, so that when deep learning showed up in 2012 with AlexNet, the infrastructure was already sitting there waiting. Nobody predicted AlexNet. The bet was simply that massive parallel compute would eventually matter to someone.

So when I think about doing that again, the lesson I take is less "build a platform" and more "find the next thing that looks like a toy today but is clearly going to need enormous compute." For me, that's physical AI. Robotics, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to act in the real world. The bottleneck there isn't language, it's that these systems need to understand physics, space, and time, and we don't have an internet-scale dataset of embodied experience. That's why we built Cosmos as world foundation models. The idea is that simulation and world models become the data engine for physical AI, the way the web was the data engine for LLMs.

And the playbook has the same shape. You make it open so researchers everywhere build on it. You accept that the first few years look unprofitable. You invest in the whole stack, not just the model, but the tools, the data pipelines, the deployment path from training to the robot or the car. And you stay humble, because the application that justifies the whole thing will probably be something you didn't predict, just as AlexNet wasn't predicted.

The honest answer is you can't engineer another CUDA directly. What you can do is recreate the conditions: a long-term conviction, a very wide distribution, and a developer community that trusts you'll still be there in ten years. Then you wait for the world to catch up.

r001.rationale: The response says CUDA was already in place when deep learning emerged, but does not identify deep learning as CUDA’s most important application.

r002.rationale: It says you “can’t engineer another CUDA directly,” rejecting the idea that repeating its original path will reproduce its success.

r003.rationale: It recommends finding the next important compute need of the present, naming physical AI as the opportunity.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to understand that CUDA’s success is not just about a programming language or a compiler. It’s about an entire ecosystem: the libraries, the tools, and the developers who have invested time in learning how to use them. Those pieces reinforce one another, and that’s very difficult to replicate by simply building a similar interface.

So I would start with the developer’s problem. Can you make an important workload substantially easier to build or more efficient to run? Can you provide a good experience all the way from writing the code to debugging and deploying it? Hardware performance matters, but developers need to be able to access that performance without doing all the work themselves.

Then you need consistency over time. People build on a platform when they trust that their investment will continue to be useful. So, to me, replicating CUDA’s success means earning that trust and building that ecosystem, rather than just matching a set of technical features.

r001.rationale: The response discusses CUDA’s ecosystem but does not say it preceded deep learning or that deep learning became its most important application.

r002.rationale: It says a similar interface is insufficient, but does not judge that following CUDA’s original development path is unlikely to reproduce its success.

r003.rationale: It recommends focusing on developer problems and building trust, but does not say efforts should adapt to the important contributions possible at a given time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to understand that CUDA’s success is about much more than the programming language or the hardware. It’s the whole ecosystem: the libraries, the tools, and the experience developers have accumulated over time. All of those pieces reinforce each other.

So if you want to replicate that success, you need to give developers a compelling reason to adopt your platform. That could start with a particular workload where you offer a substantial advantage. But performance alone isn’t enough. It has to be easy to program, easy to debug, and easy to integrate into the software people already use.

I would focus on making a specific group of developers successful first, then expand from there. An ecosystem grows because people can reliably get their work done.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses CUDA’s ecosystem and developer experience but does not say CUDA preceded deep learning or that deep learning became its most important application.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not assess whether repeating CUDA’s original development path is likely to reproduce its success.

r003.rationale: The candidate recommends focusing on a workload and developer group, but does not tie replication efforts to the important contributions possible at a given time.
